newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Gene-soya half the story behind rape oil premium.
newsitem.headline: Gene-soya half the story behind rape oil premium.

text.p: European meals and feed traders said on Thursday the high premium of rape oil in Rotterdam over soy oil was only partly down to fears over the controversial import of genetically modified soybeans from the United States.
Traders and analysts said a general tightness in the rapeseed market had left crushers short of material and as a consequence the lack of rape oil had raised its premium to soy.

But fears the new U.S. soybean imports will be unsellable to food processing companies in Europe -- some German, Austrian and Swiss firms have already said they will not sell products made from the new beans -- has exacerbated the situation, they said.

"There are two reasons for the premium." said Arie van Dijk of market statisticians Stigevo. "The main one is the tight supplies of rapeseed and then secondly, the psychological impact from genetically modified soybeans."
Van Dijk said a fall in this season's key German rapeseed crop -- down to an estimated 1.94 million tonnes from 3.1 million last year -- was the main reason for the tightness.

December rapeseed is trading firmly at around 470 marks a tonnes, a reflection of tight seed supplies as sellers slow down deliveries to crushers in a play that traders said was common for the time of year.

But the prospect of imports of the new beans are beginning to impact on the market. Van Dijk noted an increasing number of European food firms specifying usage of non-genetically altered beans. "There is definitely a trend developing," he said.

Traders said one current option to traders wishing to avoid the non-modified beans was to trade soley with material from Brazil and Argentina. But some then cited market speculation that 1997 seedlings in Latin America would also contain the new beans. One trader said he had heard that this year's crop contained "a significant amount of the new beans."
